what_its_for: This medicine is a gene therapy gel used to treat wounds called dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). DEB is a rare skin condition where your skin is very fragile and blisters or tears easily because of a missing or broken protein called collagen type VII. This gel helps your skin make more of that protein so wounds can heal better.
how_to_take: This gel is applied directly on your wounds (on the skin, not taken by mouth). A healthcare provider will usually apply it for you in a clinic or doctor's office. The gel is spread gently over each open wound and then covered with a bandage. Do not apply it to wounds near your eyes unless your doctor tells you to. Only trained healthcare providers should prepare and apply this medication.
dosing: The gel is applied to your wounds once a week. Your doctor will decide how much gel to use based on the size of your wounds. Each wound is treated separately. Your treatment schedule will be planned by your healthcare team, so follow their instructions closely.
missed_dose: If you miss your weekly treatment appointment, contact your healthcare provider as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not try to apply extra gel on your own to make up for a missed dose. Your doctor will guide you on when to come in for your next application.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or specialty pharmacy. It must be kept frozen at very cold temperatures. Do not try to store or handle this medication at home unless you have received special instructions from your healthcare team. Keep it away from children and do not use it if the packaging looks damaged or if the expiration date has passed.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are taking any medicines that suppress your immune system, since this could affect how well your body responds to the treatment. Avoid touching or rubbing the treated wound area after the gel has been applied. Do not let the treated area come into contact with other people's skin right after application, especially people who have weak immune systems, as this is a live virus-based therapy. Avoid exposing treated wounds to dirt, pool water, or anything that could cause infection.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice signs of infection at the wound site such as increased redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or a bad smell. Also call if you develop a fever, rash in new areas of your body, eye pain or redness, or any unusual pain or discomfort. Contact your doctor if someone in close contact with you, such as a family member, develops new skin sores or blisters, as the virus used in this therapy can rarely spread to others.
when_it_works: Wound healing may begin within a few weeks, but results vary from person to person. Many patients start to see wounds closing and improving after several weeks of weekly treatments. Your doctor will check your wounds regularly to see how well they are healing. It is important to keep all of your appointments even if your wounds seem to be improving.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as the safety of this medicine in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not fully known. If you or a close contact has a weakened immune system (for example, due to HIV, cancer treatment, or other immune conditions), let your doctor know before starting treatment, as there may be extra precautions needed. The safety and use in very young children and older adults should be discussed with your healthcare provider.
